        Week 6 wraps up in Santa Clara, where the Washington Commanders will visit the San Francisco 49ers for a "Monday Night Football" showdown. As Washington tries to inch closer to .500 on the season and rid itself of the sour taste of a tie with the Giants last week, it will have one of its key weapons on offense. The status of Stefon Diggs was up in the air for this primetime matchup as the wideout dealt with a hamstring injury, but he is active. Diggs did not practice at the start of the week on Thursday, but returned to practice in a limited capacity on Friday and Saturday. Officially, he was listed as questionable.Diggs, who signed a one-year deal with the franchise in early August, did not play in last week's tie with New York because of that hamstring. 

        
            
                49ers vs. Commanders prediction: Can San Francisco remain unbeaten? Full 'Monday Night Football' breakdown
                
                    Jared Dubin                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
When healthy, the 32-year-old has been a heavily involved figure within the Commanders offense, averaging just under eight targets per game so far this season. Because Terry McLaurin has also been in and out of the lineup due to injury, Diggs actually leads the team in targets (31), receptions (18), and receiving touchdowns (3). His 170 receiving yards are second to McLaurin (203). What's fascinating about Diggs' tenure so far in Washington is that he's seen minimal time playing with quarterback Jayden Daniels. Because of injuries, there's only been one full game played between the two. That came in the season-opening loss to Philadelphia, where Diggs caught four of nine targets for 55 yards and a touchdown. Before Daniels left Week 2's loss to the Cowboys with a left elbow injury, the two connected for another touchdown. If/when these two can stay healthy and be on the field at the same time, they've flashed some explosiveness. 
That'll be extremely important in this NFC matchup as the 49ers defense has been one of the stoutest in the league entering Week 6. San Francisco has the lowest explosive play rate allowed through five games by any team since 2000. Having a healthy Diggs would go a long way in putting a dent into that historic figure.

title: How Bronny James became the last survivor of Lakers' 2024 draft class -- and why that's not a good thing - CBS Sports
description: With his father on the 76ers, James still kept his Lakers roster spot over first-round pick Dalton Knecht
body:
With his father on the 76ers, James still kept his Lakers roster spot over first-round pick Dalton Knecht
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 19, 2026
                            
                    at
    7:05 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        On Monday, JJ Redick revealed that Bronny James and Dalton Knecht were both excused absences from practice on Monday. Both were ill, a statement The Athletic felt compelled to confirm in a follow-up report because, well, it seemed more like they both had a concerning case of Roster Bubble-itis. The Los Angeles Lakers spent most of the offseason with 16 players under standard contracts. Monday was the deadline to trim the roster down to 15, and the two likeliest candidates to get moved were their two 2024 draft picks.Redick himself said that he didn't think James played well in the preseason. He shot just 4-of-16 from the floor, and the Lakers lost his 82 minutes by 31 points. Yet the bar, apparently, was even lower, as it was ultimately Knecht, the No. 17 pick in that 2024 class, who was waived. All told, the pair of them and everything that has followed amounts to an abject disaster of a draft class for Rob Pelinka. Consider the following:Through two years, neither James nor Knecht have grown into NBA-caliber players. James, as a late-second round pick, was always fighting long odds. Knecht, frequently cited as the steal of that draft, was supposed to be a difference-maker early on. He entered the NBA as a 23-year-old coming off of an SEC Player of the Year season with a skill set that seemingly fit the existing roster to a tee. Aside from a few flashes early in his rookie year, he showed virtually nothing as a Laker.The Lakers tried to trade Knecht to the Charlotte Hornets. They called off the deal after failing Mark Williams' physical and could never move Knecht, or rebuild his confidence, afterward.Though they'd deny it, the Lakers surely drafted James, on some level, for the sake of preserving their relationship with his far more valuable father. Well, if Bronny was supposed to be a bridge between player and team, he failed on that front. LeBron James literally took a minimum-salary contract to play for somebody else.The Lakers didn't realize neither had a future with them quickly enough to move on last offseason when doing so would have allowed the flexibility to retain key defender Jordan Goodwin, who actually was an important part of the 2024-25 rotation and wound up breaking out for the Phoenix Suns after the Lakers let him go.The Lakers had a whole offseason to move either Knecht, James or someone else. They could have demanded it as a condition of trading nearly their entire cache of draft picks to the Utah Jazz for Walker Kessler. They could have signed one fewer free agent or made an aggregation trade. Instead, these picks went so badly that the Lakers were forced to take on the dead money that would come from waiving one of them. They couldn't even close the book on this miserable draft prooperly.At least to this point, the 2024 draft class has been a failure at every level. The Lakers picked the wrong players, developed them poorly and mismanaged the process of moving on from them. It's emblematic of many of the failures that have come under Pelinka. The Lakers land big-name players because they're the Lakers, and then they botch the margins around them.Why did the Lakers keep Bronny over Knecht?Why exactly James outlasted Knecht could come down to a number of factors. The more defensively oriented James is arguably the better fit on this offense-centric roster than Knecht, whose best trait is theoretically his shooting. James is undeniably the bigger name of the two just because of, well, his actual name. Technically speaking, the Lakers still have a LeBron James on their team. Neither played well in the preseason. We don't know what happened behind closed doors at training camp practices. James presumably outplayed Knecht there.
That doesn't mean he's proven he has an NBA future. At this point, it's getting harder and harder to believe that's the case. James simply is not an NBA-viable offensive player. Through two years, he has not proven capable of putting the ball through the hoop from anywhere on the court at the rate that a 6-foot-2 guard needs to in order to be playable. Even if he could hit the bare minimum number of shots to survive as a small, defense-first guard, it's not as though he's cleared the incredibly high bar a defender needs to in order to provide genuine value at that size. He is not a Jamal Shead-level pest. That's the standard at that size. James has never reached it.
Maybe that changes. Again, the Lakers have seen more of James, and Knecht for that matter, than we have, and it should be noted that James at least provided a handful of not-terrible minutes against the Houston Rockets in the playoffs a year ago. Development isn't linear. Maybe there's more to Bronny than we've thus far seen.
But when teams are forced to decide between two young and underwhelming players, the first-round pedigree, along with the greater cap number for the sake of trade flexibility, usually wins out. Even if there was more to the decision to keep James, it was fundamentally driven by how badly the Lakers mismanaged the Knecht situation. The Lakers bungled the 2024 draft so badly that a player who's done little to prove future NBA viability through two years had to make the team just because their other selection in that same class was worse. His continued presence on this roster, therefore, says far more about the team that drafted him than the player he's thus far become.

The Notre Dame quarterback struggled downfield against an elite defense, leaving the Irish with no room for error as an early-November clash with No. 1 Miami looms

        PROVO, Utah -- Heading into Notre Dame's star-studded matchup against BYU, quarterback CJ Carr was seen as a trump card. The junior was projected, by some, as a first-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft entering the season and one of the most talented signal-callers to come through South Bend in the modern era. Especially with relatively unheralded quarterback Bear Bachmeier on the other sideline, Carr's pedigree was viewed as a major mismatch. Instead, the gap in quarterback play proved decisive as BYU pulled off the 28-24 upset to stun Notre Dame. And suddenly, a sterling case for Carr as a quarterback becomes much more complicated. Carr came into the weekend clearing 63% completion and a 155 passer rating in every prior game this season. Against BYU, the first elite defense on the schedule, Carr looked mortal. The junior completed a career-low 55.1% of his passes, 27-of-49 overall on 5.3 yards per pass attempt. As BYU built a double-digit lead, Carr had a period of completing only 7 of 17 passes across the second and third quarters. 
"I don't know, it wasn't the preparation," Notre Dame coach Marcus Freeman said. "Some of those big plays that he usually hits, we weren't executing on. We weren't hitting them. I don't know if it's CJ's fault, I don't know if it's the wide receivers' fault or an accumulation of both." 
        
            
                Is Notre Dame in danger of missing CFP? Familiar conversation around Irish emerges after first loss of season
                
                    Brad Crawford                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Inconsistent downfieldOn the first drive of the game, Carr connected on his first three passes to drive down the field, all short passes at the edges. Then, he dropped back on third down to target a wide-open Jordan Faison streaking towards the end zone. He airmailed the pass by several yards. That didn't improve as the game went on. Carr connected on only 30.4% of his passes further than 10 yards downfield, according to Pro Football Focus. Heading into the matchup, he was hitting on 60.0% of such passes. Furthermore, Carr attempted only 7.8 passes 10+ yards downfield per game in six wins; he attempted 23 against BYU. 
BYU didn't record a sack on Carr, but he was pressured a career-high 13 times. As he tried to force the issue, Carr's performance continued to slip. Carr has done a tremendous job of performing against middling opponents. When faced with an elite defense that could force him to make difficult plays, he faltered, and Notre Dame followed. The inconsistency allowed BYU to focus on the running game, holding them to 2.4 yards per carry in the second half. The performance was in contrast to Bachmeier, who played the game of his life. The sophomore posted 224 yards passing, 45 yards rushing, 15 yards receiving and four touchdowns against the No. 1 defense in college football. Notre Dame reportedly strung Bachmeier along during the recruiting process; now he's in the top 10 in Heisman odds. 
"Out of high school, Notre Dame disrespected me and my family pretty badly," the normally quiet Bachmeier said. "There was no way I was going to lose to those guys." Notre Dame's big-game woesSince reaching the national championship game in 2024 with dual-threat Riley Leonard at quarterback, Notre Dame is 2-3 against AP Top 25 opponents with Carr at the helm. They lost all three games against teams ranked No. 16 or higher. Furthermore, Notre Dame has not beaten an AP top-10 opponent on the road since 2012, when Manti Te'o led the Irish to the national title game. 
Notre Dame has spent the Freeman era building the program into a behemoth. The Irish jumped from outside of the top 10 to No. 6 in the 247Sports Talent Composite under Freeman, and they're No. 2 in the blue-chip ratio. Notre Dame has the talent at every position to win a national championship. But in the loss to BYU -- ranked No. 53 in the talent composite -- it was execution that stood apart. "They used a lot of things that we hadn't seen on film," linebacker Drayk Bowen said. "They kind of used our weaknesses against us. Now we'll be able to go back, look at it and say, we really need to improve in these areas. It'll be a good bye week for us." 
Carr showed flashes of brilliance across the game. Notre Dame went 4-of-4 on fourth downs, which included multiple tight Carr passes. He marched the Irish down the field at the end of the game to set up a potential game-winning throw into the end zone. Notre Dame wouldn't have been close without his checks. But to reach the lofty expectations, Notre Dame needs more from its talented signal-caller. A home game against No. 1 Miami becomes a must-win, or the Irish could again find themselves outside of the College Football Playoff. "We've just gotta go back to work, do what we do, practice well all week," Carr said. "We'll try to continue to string things together through the bye week and to bounce back with whoever we've got next."

schema.headline: How CJ Carr's rough night vs. BYU raises doubts about Notre Dame's title ceiling - CBS Sports

title: Rams special teams woes continue: Kicker Blake Grupe placed on injured reserve after knee injury - CBS Sports
description: Grupe suffered the injury while making a tackle on a kickoff
body:
Grupe suffered the injury while making a tackle on a kickoff
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 19, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:59 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Los Angeles Rams' kicking conundrum continued into Week 6, but not in the way you'd expect. After cutting former placekicker Harrison Mevis after Week 5, L.A. seemingly found its solution after signing Blake Grupe to assume the kicking duties. The former Notre Dame kicker made his Rams debut on Sunday and quickly endeared himself to his new squad by netting a 44-yard field goal in the first quarter. However, things went downhill after that. Grupe left the game early after suffering a knee injury on a kickoff. On Monday, the Rams placed him on injured reserve, leaving them once again looking for a kicker. Head coach Sean McVay said Grupe tore his ACL.Grupe suffered the injury while making a tackle on the kickoff following his made field goal. He was seen lowering his shoulder to hit returner Devin Duvernay and came down awkwardly. 
With Grupe sidelined, the entire kicking operation was reshuffled. Punter Ethan Evans served as the kicker. He only attempted one kicker, a successful extra point after the Rams' fourth-quarter touchdown. 
However, otherwise, Los Angeles was hesitant to use Evans. After Matthew Stafford connected with Blake Corum for a 15-yard touchdown in the second quarter, they kept the offense on the field for a two-point attempt, which failed. Then, when they were at the Arizona 27-yard line and faced with a fourth-and-1, Los Angeles went for it, but turned the ball over on downs. Grupe entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2023, initially signing with the Saints. He played for New Orleans until midway through the 2025 season, when he was released. After that, he made stops with the Colts and Jets before finding his way to the Rams. Coming into this game, Grupe had converted 81.9% of his career field goals (86-of-105) and 98% of his extra points (96-of-98). 
The kicking game has been an issue throughout the first half of the season for the Rams, and it came to a head during Monday's overtime loss to the Bills. Mevis failed to convert on either of his field goal attempts, including what would've been a game-winner, which was blocked. That forced Los Angeles' hand to make a change in favor of Grupe, but this latest injury keeps them in a kicking nightmare.

title: Grading every NBA rookie extension: Evaluating new contracts for Victor Wembanyama, Keyonte George, more - CBS Sports
description: As the 2026 offseason draws to a close we have officially reached the NBA's Oct. 19 deadline for rookie extensions. First-round picks in
body:
As the 2026 offseason draws to a close we have officially reached the NBA's Oct. 19 deadline for rookie extensions. First-round picks in the 2023 NBA Draft were eligible to sign rookie extensions until today, and ultimately, six of them did so:No. 1 overall pick Victor Wembanyama signed a five-year, $252 million extension with the San Antonio Spurs;No. 2 overall pick Brandon Miller signed a five-year, $209 million extension with the Charlotte Hornets;No. 4 overall pick Amen Thompson signed a five-year, $208 million extension with the Houston Rockets;No. 5 overall pick Ausar Thompson signed a five-year, $155 million extension with the Detroit Pistons;No. 10 overall pick Cason Wallace signed a five-year, $139 million extension with the Oklahoma City Thunder;No. 16 overall pick Keyonte George signed a five-year, $157.5 million extension with the Utah Jazz;No. 19 overall pick Brandin Podziemski signed a five-year, $110 million extension with the Golden State Warriors.A total of seven 2023 first-round picks were not eligible for rookie extensions because they either had their fourth-year options declined or were waived earlier. The bulk of the 2023 class, however, was still eligible to negotiate, and we graded all of the deals that ultimately came.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Victor Wembanyama (No. 1 pick): A+Terms: Five years, $252 million, player option on the final yearThere is no contract Wembanyama could have signed that would not have represented an enormous organizational victory for the Spurs. The best player in the NBA in his early 20s, or really at any point in his career, always has one of the league's best contracts because the absolute top of the market is restricted by the very concept of a max salary. Nikola Jokić is underpaid even at 35% of the cap. LeBron James was underpaid for virtually his entire career. There's no amount you can pay someone this good that isn't team-friendly.Yet Wembanyama's deal is especially notable because this isn't necessarily his max. Wembanyama signed a contract that will start him at 25% of the cap and include the standard 8% annual raises thereafter. For most players, this is indeed a max contract. However, Wembanyama could have included Rose Rule escalators in his deal that would have vaulted that starting salary to 30% of the cap if he were to win MVP or Defensive Player of the Year, or make an All-NBA Team this season. If he reaches the 65-game requirement, he is a virtual lock to do so.
We've seen other players, most notably Tyrese Haliburton, play through injuries in ways that proved detrimental over the longer term for the sake of ensuring eligibility for that Rose Rule bump. The Spurs have been notoriously cautious with Wembanyama's health thus far in his career, and justifiably so given his uncommon physical proportions. If Wembanyama had wanted the 30% max, the Spurs would have given it to him, and they almost certainly would not have stood in his way if he'd attempted to make medical decisions that steered him towards eligibility. The easiest way to burn a bridge with a player is to cost him money. Now, the Spurs won't have to worry about that. They can be as cautious as they want, knowing Wembanyama has nothing to gain by playing when he shouldn't.If Wembanyama is merely as good as he was at the end of last season for the duration of this deal, it's one of the best contracts in the NBA. If he improves in all of the ways that we suspect he should, it rises to the level that some of the best LeBron contracts did as an all-time value deal, even despite a max or max-adjacent price tag. Injury is the only concern here, but it's not enough of one to lower this grade. Any team in the NBA would have been thrilled to sign Wembanyama to this contract.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Brandon Miller (No. 2): B+Terms: Five years, $209 millionMiller, more than any other player in this class, exemplifies how rookie extension negotiations have changed in recent years. Think of how many promising yet ultimately unaccomplished top draft picks used to get blind maxes. Franz Wagner, for instance. Michael Porter Jr. Andrew Wiggins. If you were drafted in the lottery and showed even the faintest whiff of future stardom, especially as a wing, it was just a no-brainer. You got maxed. Miller didn't. 
He didn't come all that close, either. While we don't yet know the contract's structure (and Charlotte has the flexibility to get creative on that front), the lowest possible starting point would come in between 20% and 21% of next year's projected cap. The max extension for most players in this experience bracket would start them at 25%. The Hornets seemingly negotiated down to the final minutes before Monday's deadline and secured some of the more favorable terms you'll ever see on a player of Miller's ilk. With LaMelo Ball gone, he and Kon Knueppel are the franchise players now. He's a No. 2 overall pick at the NBA's most valuable position coming off of a breakout season, yet when you adjust for inflation, he's making less than Brandon Ingram on his current deal.Ingram is the worst-case scenario for Miller from an archetypal standpoint. They can both get too jumper-heavy, though Miller's, thankfully, tend to come from behind the arc. Ingram has flashed considerable defensive upside at points but never sustained it. Miller took a real step on that front a year ago, but he has further to go if Charlotte is going to survive with its relatively undersized front court. Miller has improved noticeably in each of his NBA seasons. Life without Ball is going to get harder, and that's the test here. Almost 63% of Miller's shots were assisted a year ago. A lot of Ball's creation burden is now going to fall on his shoulders. Miller has to get to the rim and the line more. He'll have to grow as a passer too, especially with all of the doubles he's about to see in his post-Ball world. Today, this contract is fine. It becomes a steal if Miller grows into the more well-rounded cornerstone the Hornets are hoping he can be.
But one of the benefits of taking a step back, as Charlotte did this season, was that it gives players like Miller more room to experiment and develop. He's in a friendly environment to do so given all of the shooting Charlotte has accumulated. This is his team now, and if that works out as well as Charlotte hopes, getting him this far below the max could create one of the better contracts in basketball.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Amen Thompson (No. 4): B-Terms: Five years, $208 millionThe Thompson twins are tricky to value because they really don't have any appropriate points of comparison. In Amen's case specifically, the closest you could probably come is Dyson Daniels on his $25 million-per-year contract. Thompson is just shy of $42 million annually, but he's better at just about everything. The Thompsons are the two best non-center defenders in the NBA, save perhaps Alex Caruso, whose load gets managed pretty aggressively by the Oklahoma City Thunder. Daniels is a decent rebounder, solid playmaker and great transition player. Amen is better than him at all of those things.The hope coming into last season, especially with Fred VanVleet injured, was that Thompson could use those extra on-ball reps to grow into something resembling Russell Westbrook: the nuclear athlete who made up for his limitations as a shooter by getting to the rim at will. It hasn't happened yet, though Houston's low-shooting ecosystem and uninspiring offensive scheme certainly played a role there. Thompson bears some responsibility here as well. He has work to do as a ball-handler and finisher. He doesn't have Westbrook's preternatural aggression, though that's hardly a fair standard to hold anyone to.
What we mostly established last season was that Thompson is more wing than point guard, even if he has some point guard traits. It's easier to get away with lacking a jump shot when the ball is in your hands and the offense is running through you. There aren't exactly recent examples of teams winning championships with Thompson-esque players making more than 20% of the cap. More often, players who share a few of his traits -- Caruso with his defense and supplementary playmaking, Josh Hart with his rebounding and transition excellence -- are making a lot less money and at least offering some sort of 3-point threat.Thompson is an anomaly in this respect. We're not used to teams making this sort of bet on a player like him, though players like him hardly even exist. The modern NBA is perhaps a bit friendlier to players like him than the one we lived in even, say, five years ago. The possession game is king now, and players who can generate turnovers, own the offensive glass and dominate in transition are worth their weight in gold. The Rockets were at the forefront of that shift. This is a bet on their team-building philosophy as much as it is on Thompson, specifically.Thompson's absurd athleticism, matched in the current NBA only by his brother, will have to hold up through his late-20s for this contract to work. He'll have to grow as an on-ball scorer as well, perhaps not to Westbrook's level, but certainly beyond the 20 points per game threshold. Those are reasonable goals, though, and Houston is asset-rich enough to tailor a roster to Thompson's needs. The Rockets aren't in their final form yet, but tailoring that eventual roster around a player as singularly gifted as Thompson is ultimately the right decision. This deal isn't without its risks, but all in all, it's a reasonable figure.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Ausar Thompson (No. 5): BTerms: Five years, $155 millionWe may not have a helpful out-of-family comparison for the Thompson twins, but their deals compare interestingly against one another. They cover the same term, but Ausar will make just under 75% of what Amen makes in that time frame. Ausar might genuinely be the only non-center in the NBA who could credibly argue to be a level above Amen defensively, though Amen's greater offensive workload plays a role there. There was a real argument that among non-Wembanyama mortals, Ausar Thompson was the NBA's best defender last season. After Game 7 of Detroit's second-round loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers, Kenny Atkinson noted that "the tactical adjustment we made was avoiding Thompson. We were just like, if he's near the ball, throw it to someone else." The tracking data more than supports that notion. Donovan Mitchell shot 5-of-20 in the series with Thompson as his primary defender. James Harden was 0-for-8. Oh yeah, and he had nine blocks, 12 steals and 28 deflections in the series. Ausar does everything on defense. He is genuinely transformative on that end of the floor. He's just far behind his brother as an on-ball offensive player. He still brings the offensive rebounding. He's getting better as a secondary playmaker and he's a willing cutter, but he's such a limited scoring threat that his presence can be a real offensive drag. Jalen Suggs only loosely pretended to guard him in the first round of the playoffs, and that's a big reason the Orlando Magic nearly toppled the Pistons in a humiliating No. 1 vs. No. 8 first-round matchup.The first and most important question for non-point guard perimeter players offensively is shooting. Neither Thompson has yet developed any sort of 3-point shot. You're employing them for mostly the same reasons, starting with defense. Would you want to pay a roughly $10 million annual premium for that star defender to have some on-ball juice? That depends on a dozen factors. If the Rockets think Amen still has offensive star potential, the answer is yes. I've grown pretty dubious on that front. I think it's likelier that Ausar sneaks closer to Amen's level now.
They're ultimately going to function similarly within your roster construction. You're still going to have to surround both with more shooting and creation than their teams have so far. Those things are expensive. With that in mind, I think by a hair I'd rather pay Ausar than upgrade to the premium model. The flexibility to surround these two with the sort of teammates they'll need is paramount, and since I'm getting the most important traits out of both, that $53 million gap is just enough that I think the Pistons did slightly better in their deal with a Thompson twin.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Cason Wallace (No. 10): B+Terms: Five years, $139 millionNo team was under more pressure to secure an extension with their 2023 draftee than the Thunder. Normally, teams hesitate to tender offer sheets in free agency because they are almost always matched. But the whole league knows how tight Oklahoma City's finances are, and everyone would love to weaken the NBA's best roster. Wallace was therefore a near-lock to not only secure an offer sheet, but one that was structured as inconveniently as possible for the Thunder. Throw in his new starting role and the possible elevation in value that will come with it, and the Thunder did very well to secure Wallace before the season began.The initial value of the contract is strong. Remember, Wallace, like both Thompson twins, has made an All-Defensive team. He's not the on-ball player that Amen is and he's not nearly as versatile defensively as either of them given the vast size disparity, but he has the one trait they're both dying for: a somewhat reliable 3-point shot. Considering none figure to be primary shot-creators at any point in their career, you could argue that is the single most desirable offensive trait any star defender of their ilk could have. Wallace has it, and he's making less than both of them. We throw around the term "3-and-D" wing so frequently for a reason, folks.
Wallace obviously is not quite a wing. He can't guard up the positional spectrum like the Thompsons can and he'll never be the rim-protector that they are either. But he's a relentless on-ball pest who generates among the most turnovers in basketball at a point at which turnover-generation has never been a more valuable trait. Even if he's not the game-breaker that the Thompsons can be defensively, the gap is relatively small, and if Wallace never grows offensively, his shooting affords so much more lineup and roster-building flexibility than either of the Thompsons offer.And then of course, we have to acknowledge the chance that Wallace does grow offensively. This is his first crack at a full-time starting role, but he thrived in a small sample with a higher-usage role a season ago. In a nine-game stretch that Shai Gilgeous-Alexander missed a season ago, Wallace averaged just under 15 points and over five assists per game despite relatively weak 3-point shooting. He's never going to be a primary creator or anything close to it. He lacks the tight handle or first step and he never gets to the line. But he showcased real growth as an individual scorer, and if he can build on that as a permanent starter while maintaining the role player skill set that got him here, this contract has a chance to become a meaningful bargain.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Keyonte George (No. 16): A-Terms: Five years, $157.5 millionThere are real holes to poke in George's game. There are notable metrics that considered him the NBA's worst defender last season, and even the friendlier ones acknowledge that he is extremely vulnerable. He needs to become more of a point guard than a pure scorer. The only players to average as many turnovers as he did last season with fewer assists were forwards: Paolo Banchero and Jaylen Brown. 
With Darryn Peterson coming in, Ace Bailey stepping into a bigger role and just the general reality that this team is now trying to win, there are going to be fewer on-ball opportunities available. From a scoring perspective, that should suit George fine. He's easily scalable as a ball-handler and the Jazz got plenty out of him off of the ball last season. But playmaking is a real necessity here, and growth from George will be the first place the Jazz look to try to find it.Got that out of the way? Cool. Getting this level of scoring from a player this young who showed so much improvement last season would have been borderline unimaginable under previous collective bargaining agreements. George's deal projects to start at 16.31% of the 2027-28 salary cap, according to Spotrac. Think of other notable defensively deficient scoring guards who have extended over the past few years: Tyler Herro started at just below 20%, Jordan Poole just above it, and Jalen Green was closer to 22%. George outscored and out-assisted all three of them in their third seasons. He admittedly did that on a tanking team with plenty of shots at his disposal, but only Poole was more efficient, and that's hardly a fair comparison since, you know, he was playing with Stephen Curry.
You could credibly argue that George is more promising today than any of them were when they signed their rookie extensions... and his contract actually gets cheaper over time on a relative basis. Herro, Poole and Green all received or came close to the maximum 8% annual raises. George is getting 4% annually, so if you assume the cap continues to grow at roughly its current rate, his deal will end at 15.56% of the cap.There is reasonable skepticism about how valuable George will be moving forward. He has to improve in a few key areas, and the NBA is moving away from smaller, all-offense guards. But George is making far less than most of the players of that archetype, and that's before we even consider the max-adjacent deals players like Austin Reaves and Trae Young just got. If this doesn't work out, the numbers are low enough that the deal remains tradable. Utah might simply find that George isn't the right sort of backcourt mate to pair with Peterson anyway. But a player this young and this talented has a chance to be a genuine steal on a contract like this, and for a Jazz team that's suddenly getting pretty expensive, contractual victories like that are an absolute necessity.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Brandin Podziemski (No. 19): CTerms: Five years, $110 million, mutual option on the final yearBrandin Podziemski is a good player. He's a jack of all trades who affects games in a number of subtle ways. He's a great rebounder for his position. He draws charges. He's a solid enough defender who tends to rate better through the all-in-one metrics than the eye test, mostly because his strengths are off the ball. He'll make 3s and he'll create a bit of offense and you'll rarely have to worry about him when he's on the floor. But he doesn't exactly have a calling card either. He's not a point guard-level shot-creator. He's not an elite 3-point shooter or point-of-attack defender.When you're negotiating with someone you expect to be a cornerstone of your future, it makes sense to prioritize getting a deal done even if the terms aren't perfect. Maintaining your relationships with such players matters. But when you go a bit further down the organizational totem pole, it behooves you to negotiate as hard as possible on rookie extensions. The entire deck is stacked in your favor as a team in these negotiations. The player in question hasn't made much money yet. Restricted free agency works against them finding fair market value in the following summer. One injury can derail their long-term earning power. With players like this, it only really makes sense to sign a rookie extension when you're getting great value.What would have to happen for Golden State to get great value on these terms? Since Podziemski doesn't have those premium skills, he'd probably have to grow into an above-average starter when he's thus far been closer to a strong third guard. Such growth is possible, especially with reports out of training camp sounding quite positive. The money here is nearly identical to what Ayo Dosunmu got from the Minnesota Timberwolves, but remember, Dosunmu's contract was negotiated under entirely different circumstances. He was coming off of a strong playoff run, he had the leverage of unrestricted free agency and his team had just invested in the injury-prone LaMelo Ball as their starting point guard, making a pricey backup a necessity. Podziemski had none of those advantages.Spending money in restricted free agency is an enormous risk. It requires tying up your cap space through the relevant portion of free agency while knowing that it may all be for nothing if the incumbent team matches. Teams are understandably more enthusiastic about doing it for players with singular, high-value traits. You need point guard-level creation and elite point-of-attack defense to win at the highest levels, so teams take bigger risks to get it. As helpful as the things Podziemski does can be in the right context, they're not the sort of things teams tend to go far out of their way for. Barring a breakout fourth season, it was just hard to imagine someone throwing a bigger offer sheet at Podziemski than this. The Warriors probably could have squeezed him for a better deal by taking this into next summer. We've spent three years hearing about how highly the Warriors organization regards Podziemski. Maybe they're right and this turns out to be a value contract. At this moment, though, it seems as if they're paying for the player they want him to be rather than the one he's thus far proven capable of being. That doesn't necessarily make this a bad contract. It's probably par for the course for a high-end sixth man moving forward, which is where I'd expect Podziemski to fall. But these other extensions range from somewhat to extremely team-friendly in large part because the teams in question were able to successfully weaponize the harsh realities of restricted free agency into great terms. The Warriors didn't do that, and in the "every dollar counts" era the aprons have created, that may one day come back to haunt them.

title: Colts' fire GM Chris Ballard: What fire sale could look like if Indy trades DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson, others - CBS Sports
description: The Colts don't have a 2027 first-round pick. But what could they get for top veterans in preparation for a 2027
body:
The Colts don't have a 2027 first-round pick. But what could they get for top veterans in preparation for a 2027 rebuild?
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 19, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:44 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Chris Ballard era as the Indianapolis Colts general manager came to an end on Monday. A 26-20 home loss against the previously 0-5 Tennessee Titans in Week 6 was enough for Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon to pull the plug on Ballard six games into his 10th season on the job.Under Ballard, Indianapolis reached the playoffs twice (2018 and 2020), going 1-2 in those two trips. The Colts' 72-82-1 regular season record under his management ranked 17th in the league during Ballard's tenure. Indianapolis's five missed playoffs in a row (since 2021) is the Colts' longest such streak since 1988 to 1994, and the team never won an AFC South title under Ballard.Now, the franchise is left to pick up the pieces with a 2027 rebuild on the horizon. The good news is that the 2027 NFL Draft is widely regarded as one of the most talented in years. The bad news is that the Colts don't have a first-round pick thanks to trading their 2026 and 2027 first-round draft choices, as well as wide receiver Adonai Mitchell, to the New York Jets in exchange for All-Pro cornerback Sauce Gardner last season.However, there are multiple ways for Indianapolis to recoup draft capital through veterans on tradable deals. Let's take a look at what a potential fire sale of three of the Colts' top players could look like. 
DT DeForest Buckner
Three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner all but demanded a trade after the team's Week 6 loss against the Tennessee Titans. "I'm sick and tired of the same song and dance every year," Buckner told reporters postgame on Sunday.   At 32 years old, Buckner still has plenty of gas in the tank. His 4.0 sacks through six weeks are tied for the 10th most in the NFL, while his 19 quarterback pressures rank as the seventh most among defensive tackles in 2026. The Colts would be unwise not to make him available, as he is set to become a free agent in the 2027 offseason. What could his market look like?
For a player at his age and contract status, this could be one of his last prime seasons, but for legitimate contenders, that could be worth a third-or fourth-round pick. Teams who could be interested could include the Green Bay Packers (4-2), the San Francisco 49ers (5-0) and the Minnesota Vikings (5-0). The Packers lost defensive tackle Javon Hargrave for the season with a torn Achilles, so it would make sense for them to place a call for Buckner. The 49ers make too much sense. That's where Buckner played his first four seasons, culminating in the 49ers losing Super Bowl LIV to the Kansas City Chiefs to conclude the 2019 season. He was traded to the Colts for a first-round pick in the 2020 offseason. San Francisco is going through its regularly scheduled injury catastrophe, which has hit their defensive line hard. If the Vikings want a mentor for rookie first-round pick Caleb Banks and another high-level contributor for defensive coordinator Brian Flores to get creative with, they would make sense as a win-now team. LG Quenton Nelson
Colts left guard Quenton Nelson, an eight-time Pro Bowler and a three-time first-team All-Pro, is primed to be one of the NFL's most coveted free agents next offseason ahead of his 31st birthday on March 19. This season, Nelson is currently Pro Football Focus' highest-graded guard in the entire NFL with an 89.2 offensive grade. 
He is a big fish who could net the Colts a second-round pick or perhaps a first-round choice if the bidding for his services gets frisky at the trade deadline. The complication is that he would be a rental or someone who would demand a top-of-the-market extension for whoever trades for his services. Who could line up for him? The Packers, a team that has been playing mix-and-match with an injury-plagued front, have stabilized their offensive line with the same starting five combination. But they could be in the mix, since they're currently rolling with aging veterans they signed off the street to start for them. If the Houston Texans (2-4), winners of two in a row, continue to climb, perhaps they would be interested. However, their asking price could be higher since they're a fellow AFC South team. The Vikings could be interested if they want to upgrade for undrafted free agent Joe Huber at left guard, with Donovan Jackson out with a torn meniscus. The 49ers, who are currently starting 2025 seventh-round pick Connor Colby at left guard, could make an all-in trade for Nelson. 
RB Jonathan Taylor 
The Colts don't need to trade three-time Pro Bowl running back Jonathan Taylor. He is still just 27 years old, and he re-signed with Indianapolis on a two-year extension worth $44 million with $39 million in total guarantees in August. However, if the Colts want to jumpstart their rebuild in earnest, parting with Taylor now could perhaps net them a first-round pick. They could point toward the impact top-end running backs Kenneth Walker III, Bijan Robinson, Jahmyr Gibbs and others are having all around the league as reason to demand a 2027 or a 2028 first-round pick in return.Indianapolis could perhaps engage two AFC North teams, the Cincinnati Bengals (3-2) and the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2), in a bidding war. The Bengals are averaging the fifth-fewest rushing yards per game (82.8) in the entire league this season, while Aaron Rodgers could use more support for the Steelers' 13th-worst running game (99.2 rushing yards per game) in what appears to be his NFL swan song. The Packers trading a 2028 first and another pick or two for Taylor could give them the runway to release Josh Jacobs after some legal trouble landed him on the commissioner's exempt list for the first six weeks of the 2026 season. They rank dead last in the league in rushing (59.8 rushing yards per game), and Taylor is a former Wisconsin Badger. Trading for him would earn them public relations bonus points by dumping Jacobs and bringing a local product home.

title: Serie A hot takes: It's time for Juventus and Napoli to find new coaches after rough starts - CBS Sports

Elsewhere, Lazio are still one of the most surprising sides of the season so far

        It was a challenging weekend of Serie A soccer in Italy, where both Juventus and Napoli were defeated and their coaches are now seriously risking their jobs, which will depend on their performances in the next matches. Lazio and Inter are still leading the standings, with the side led by Gennaro Gattuso still being the biggest surprise of the season so far. AS Roma reacted after a disappointing Champions League game against Real Madrid and won against Genoa at the Stadio Olimpico. Now, time for some hot takes. Don't miss all the Serie A action all season long across Paramount+, CBS Sports Network and CBS Sports Golazo Network. From Italy's biggest teams to America's biggest stars Serie A has it all, and Paramount+ is the home for every minute of the action until a Scudetto winner is crowned. Massimo Allegri is in trouble The Azzurri head coach is now seriously risking losing his job after Napoli lost on Saturday against Venezia away. The home side won their first match of the season after six defeats and after appointing Davide Nicola as the new head coach. Napoli have only collected 10 points in seven games so far and lost the two opening matches of their Champions League campaign. This is why Napoli need to react against Bodo/Glimt before facing AS Roma on the weekend: Two key matches not only for the manager but also for the current campaign of the Italian team. If they don't pick up better results, Allegri might seriously risk losing his job again. 
Luciano Spalletti to be sacked? Elsewhere, things are not going so well at Juventus, where coach Luciano Spalletti is also facing the risk of losing his job after losing 3-0 at their home stadium against Lazio. Clearly, it was a disappointing start to the season for the Italian giants who only collected 11 points and three wins in the opening seven Serie A games. Spalletti seemed quite nervous after the game on Sunday, as he admitted to DAZN, "A side lacking rhythm, ideas, intensity, and commitment. There were far too many attitudes and behaviours that I didn't like." Words that should worry not only the fans but also the club that decided to commit to the Italian coach in the summer after a positive stint in the second part of the 2025-2026 season when Spalletti replaced Igor Tudor at the beginning of the previous campaign.  
Lazio are serious contenders
Let Gattuso dream. Lazio have been the most surprising side in the first part of the 2026-2027 campaign as the Biancocelesti won six matches and only drew once so far under the former Italian national team manager, and they can win it all. Lazio endured a challenging summer, with financial restrictions forcing the club to sell players before they could bring in new signings. On top of that, the ongoing fan protest against the ownership has left the Stadio Olimpico largely deserted during home games, with Lazio supporters staying away. Despite these challenges, Lazio have delivered so far, and Gattuso appeared pleased with what he had seen, while making it clear that he expects even more going forward.
"We've built a real family here, and credit must go to the club. We had to work with a limited budget in the transfer market, focusing on bringing in good people and building a strong team spirit. Now, our focus shifts to Parma. We have to take it one game at a time, and if we do that, perhaps we can surprise a few people," he said.

title: NFL suspends Bills' C.J. Gardner-Johnson for spitting on Brock Bowers - CBS Sports
description: Gardner-Johnson was ejected during Sunday's game vs. the Raiders and will forfeit money and playing time
body:
Gardner-Johnson was ejected during Sunday's game vs. the Raiders and will forfeit money and playing time
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 19, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:33 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        C.J. Gardner-Johnson will face discipline from the NFL after spitting on Brock Bowers during the Buffalo Bills' Week 6 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. On Monday, the NFL suspended the Buffalo safety for one game without pay for an act of unsportsmanlike conduct. Gardner-Johnson will miss the Bills' Week 8 game against the Baltimore Ravens. Gardner-Johnson was ejected after spitting on Bowers as he walked away during the second quarter. According to the NFL, his actions violated Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to "any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship."   
Because the Bills are in their bye week, Gardner-Johnson's suspension won't begin until Monday, October 26. He will be eligible to return to the Bills' active roster the following Monday ahead of their Week 9 road game against the Minnesota Vikings. Gardner-Johnson may appeal the suspension, but it's currently unknown whether he intends to do so. He issued an apology after the game through his Instagram page. 
"My passion and competitive nature have always been a huge part of who I am, but I also understand that there is a line that should never be crossed," he wrote. "The gesture I made toward my opponent was inappropriate, unnecessary, and not a reflection of the respect I have for him or this game. There is no excuse for my actions, and I take full accountability. No matter how emotional or intense the competition gets, I have to hold myself to a higher standard."  The NFL has taken a firmer stance on players spitting on one another since Broncos linebacker Bill Romanowski's infamous spit on 49ers wideout J.J. Stokes during a Monday night game in 1997. While he was fined $7,500 and received a stern letter from the league, Romanowski did not miss any games. He ultimately helped the Broncos win their first Super Bowl that season. Last season, Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter was fined $57,222 (the equivalent of a game check) and was ejected after spitting on Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott prior to Philadelphia's season-opening win over Dallas. The league decided not to suspend Carter for an additional game. 
An eight-year veteran, Gardner-Johnson is in the middle of his first season with the Bills. While he has played for six teams, Gardner-Johnson is best known for his two seasons with the Eagles. He had a league-high six interceptions in 2022 while helping the Eagles become NFC Champions. In 2024 (following a season in Detroit), Gardner-Johnson had six interceptions for the eventual Super Bowl champs.

title: Where to watch 49ers vs. Commanders: TV channel, live stream, odds, prediction for 'MNF' - CBS Sports

body:
San Francisco can improve to 6-0 and strengthen its NFC West lead, while Washington enters Levi's Stadium looking to pull off a sizable road upset

        In the Week 6 edition of "Monday Night Football," the San Francisco 49ers play host to the Washington Commanders.San Francisco is riding high atop the NFC West with a 5-0 record, having defeated the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks in a barnburner last week. The Niners have battled injuries on both sides of the ball all season, yet have remained unbeaten. They can create a three-game lead in the division with a victory on Monday night.Washington is coming off an absolute debacle last Sunday against the New York Giants, wherein the Commanders had a chance to kick a field goal to win the game at the end of overtime, but bungled the clock management as badly as any team you'll ever see. The Commies are just 1-3-1 entering this game, and they're looking to avoid falling further into the basement in the NFC East.Will the Niners continue to roll, or will the Commanders pull off the upset? We'll find out soon enough. Before we break down the matchup, here's a look at how you can watch the game.
Where to watch 49ers vs. Commanders liveDate: Monday, Oct. 19 | Time: 8:15 p.m. ETLocation: Levi's Stadium (Santa Clara, California)TV: ESPN/ABC | Streaming: Fubo (try for free)Follow: CBS Sports AppOdds: 49ers -7.5, O/U 52.5 via DraftKings SportsbookWhen the Commanders have the ballJayden Daniels looked no worse for wear last week in his return from another dislocated elbow. He completed 17 of 25 passes for 199 yards, while also rushing nine times for 103 yards and two touchdowns. Had he and the entire offense not totally brain-farted at the end of overtime, it would have been a wildly encouraging performance for Washington's rest-of-season outlook.While Daniels has been excellent when taking off to run in his three starts, Washington's running backs have been extremely inefficient on the ground. Jacory Croskey-Merritt (who was ruled out for this game after not practicing all week), Rachaad White, Austin Ekeler and the recently-released Kaytron Allen have combined to average just 3.7 yards per carry. The offensive line has created little push up front, with the backs collectively gaining just 0.95 yards before contact per carry, according to Tru Media, and the backs themselves have broken tackles at the second-lowest rate in all of football.The 49ers, meanwhile, have allowed just 3.7 yards per rush to enemy running backs, with great tackling being the primary method of limiting yardage. Backs have gained 1.47 yards per carry before contact (an above-average mark), but only 2.22 yards after contact thanks to the lowest broken-tackle rate in the league. As a result, San Francisco has allowed only two explosive runs all season, per Tru Media, the fewest in the NFL.
San Francisco has also been mostly strong against the pass, checking in 10th in opponents' EPA per dropback and 5th in opponents' success rate. The 49ers have allowed quarterbacks to complete only 64.4% of their passes at an average of 6.1 yards per attempt, with just five touchdowns and three interceptions in five games.  It's tough to know what to make of Washington's passing game because it hasn't been at full strength for most of the season. Daniels missed two-and-a-half games. Chig Okonwko missed two. Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs each missed one and saw their snaps limited in another. The Daniels-McLaurin-Diggs trio has shared the field for only 57 plays so far this season, according to Tru Media. Daniels is just 15 of 30 for 129 yards on those plays, but he has thrown for three scores and scrambled for 62 yards.Daniels should, in theory, see at least some clean pockets with the 49ers again playing without Nick Bosa, but Washington's offensive line has yielded pressure on over 38% of dropbacks so far this season, so the Niners could have a chance to get into Daniels' lap and force him into tough throws and mistakes. With the generally sticky coverage the San Francisco corners have played so far this season, it could be tough sledding for Washington in the passing game on Monday night.
When the 49ers have the ballSan Francisco has been the league's fourth-most efficient offense by EPA per play, according to Tru Media, ranking second with the pass and 14th with the run. Brock Purdy is playing at as high a level as any quarterback in football, completing 69% of his passes at an average of 8.4 yards per attempt with a league-high 13 touchdown passes and just two interceptions. Purdy also has a 57.9% passing success rate, which ranks as the best in the league.Purdy has done that despite hemorrhaging wide receivers throughout the season. Ricky Pearsall was lost for the year in training camp. Christian Kirk (listed as questionable for this week) has yet to make his 49er debut. De'Zhaun Stribling was injured in Week 1. Demarcus Robinson went down in Week 2. Deebo Samuel and Jacob Cowing were knocked out of last week's win over the Seahawks. Mike Evans has been playing through a painful rib injury. (He's also questionable for Monday night.) George Kittle spent the first two weeks ramping up to a full workload after last season's Achilles tear. And yet, here the 49ers are. Washington, meanwhile, has been one of the league's friendliest pass defenses. Every team the Commanders have faced has thrown for at least 257 net yards. Four of the five teams have gone more than 300 and two of them exceeded 400. The Commanders have allowed opponents to complete 65.2% of passes at an average of 7.1 yards per attempt, with 14 touchdowns and just three interceptions. The 103.9 passer rating against the Commanders to date is the sixth-worst mark in the league. It's very easy to see San Francisco finding success through the air so long as Evans suits up for the game.
Christian McCaffrey is sharing the workload in the run game far more this season than in years past, with 61 carries for 286 yards againt Kaelon Black's 37 carries for 136 yards. McCaffrey's 4.7 yards-per-carry average is far better than what he posted over the last two years (4.0 and 3.9), and his rushing success rate of 45.9% is seventh-best out of 48 qualifying running backs. That figure is the second-best mark of his career, behind only the 2023 season, during which he led the NFL in rushing yards.The Commanders have actually been stingy against the run this year, allowing only 3.9 yards per carry, with opposing backs limited to 0.69 yards per attempt before contact by the defensive front. Washington having similar success stopping the run here is important because it could make the 49ers one-dimensional, but the Commanders' pass-funnel defense also plays right into San Francisco's hands because of how efficient the 49ers' passing game has been so far this year. Purdy and Co. should eat, even if McCaffrey doesn't. PredictionI picked against the 49ers last week and regretted it almost immediately after seeing how their offense struggled against the stingy Seattle defense. Needless to say, Washington's defense is not of the same quality. I know the 49ers are still hemorrhaging wide receivers, but as long as Brock Purdy, Mike Evans, George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey are healthy and Kyle Shanahan is calling the plays, they are going to move the ball efficiently. And I don't trust the Commanders to do quite enough to keep up with their explosive offense.  Pick: 49ers 27, Commanders 16

title: Dalton Knecht waived by Lakers: Why the 2024 draft class was doomed from the start (and the No. 1 pick) - CBS Sports
description: The 2023 NBA Draft featured Victor Wembanyama, who many already consider the best player in the world. The 2025 Draft had an epic tank b
body:
The 2023 NBA Draft featured Victor Wembanyama, who many already consider the best player in the world. The 2025 Draft had an epic tank battle to "Capture the Flagg" in order to secure Cooper Flagg. And of course, the 2026 Draft — despite none of the players playing a single regular-season minute yet — has the potential to go down as one of the greatest classes in NBA history.Between those draft classes, you have the 2024 Draft. In the months leading up to the event, it was, at least on paper, viewed as an underwhelming class compared with previous years and the drafts to follow. It lacked both consensus and blue-chip talent, unlike the top of the 2023, 2025, and 2026 classes.Through the first two seasons, the data doesn't lie. Four lottery picks from the class have already been traded, including No. 1 overall pick Zaccharie Risacher. Kel'el Ware and Jared McCain, the No. 15 and 16 picks in the draft, respectively, were also traded, albeit for different reasons. 
        
            
                Ranking the NBA's top 100 players: Victor Wembanyama enters 2026-27 season at No. 1
                
                    Sam Quinn                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
And Dalton Knecht, who showed promise during his lone season at Tennessee in 2023-24 as a potential draft riser, was waived by the Lakers on Monday, according to ESPN. Knecht had been in trade rumors since his rookie season, which included a botched trade at the 2024 trade deadline that would've seen him go to the Hornets in exchange for Mark Williams.
While yes, this class hasn't exactly been Hall of Fame-worthy, there have been some bright spots. Stephon Castle looks like a legitimate star. Donovan Clingan, Alex Sarr, and Zach Edey are all starting-level bigs in the NBA. Matas Buzelis would probably go top 5 in a re-draft. And you can't forget about the steal of the draft: Ajay Mitchell. The Thunder guard was one of the stars of the 2026 playoffs and checked in at No. 86 in our CBS Sports Top 100 NBA player list. Sarr (No. 94), Castle (No. 40), and Mitchell were the lone members of the 2024 draft class who cracked the list.With so much uncertainty surrounding the class, let's dive into what went wrong, what's next, and why this class can be a cautionary tale for next summer's draft.
Why the uncertainty of the class started at No. 1 with AtlantaOnly three No. 1 overall picks this century have been traded before the start of their third NBA season. Risacher is one of them, and he isn't in exactly prestigious company.Anthony Bennett (2013): To this day, Bennett going No. 1 is one of the most shocking moments in draft history. The UNLV big man appeared in just 52 games for the Cavaliers before being traded to the Timberwolves. The 2013 Draft remains the lowlight of this century. Then again, the Bucks selected a teenager from Greece named Giannis Antetokounmpo with the No. 15 pick. It's safe to say that pick worked out well.Markelle Fultz (2017): After playing just 33 total regular-season games with the 76ers, Fultz was traded to the Magic. He spent five seasons in Orlando, then moved on to the Kings (21 games) and Raptors (5) and is currently unsigned. Fultz was picked ahead of the likes of Jayson Tatum (No. 3), De'Aaron Fox (No. 5), Lauri Markkanen (No. 7), Donovan Mitchell (No. 13) and Bam Adebayo (No. 14).Zaccharie Risacher (2024): There was debate about what the Hawks would do in the weeks leading up to this draft. The three options were Risacher, Sarr and Reed Sheppard. Notably, Sarr did not work out with the Hawks, which cleared the way for Atlanta to make Risacher the pick. He was traded after just two seasons to the Mavericks, where he will team up with Flagg, the No. 1 overall pick selected the year after him.Risacher wasn't exactly a can't-miss prospect. The 6-foot-8 wing had the archetype and upside as a shooter that NBA decision-makers covet, but it just didn't work for him in Atlanta. After a promising rookie season during which he averaged 12.6 points, 3.6 rebounds and shot 35.5% from the 3-point line on 4.6 attempts per game, his overall volume decreased as a sophomore.During the first round of the playoffs against the Knicks, Risacher found himself out of the rotation after Game 1 and played just 22 total minutes across three games. The writing was on the wall, given Atlanta's plethora of players at the same position, and Risacher was be the odd man out.
Now, Risacher will try to revive his career in his second act with the Mavericks. If there is any consolation prize, new Mavericks coach Dusty May has experience working with jumbo lineups, which could bode well for Risacher. During his final season at Michigan, May started three frontcourt players: Aday Mara, Morez Johnson Jr., and Yaxel Lendeborg. The year before that, Michigan was the only team in college basketball that started two 7-footers: Danny Wolf and Vlad Goldin.
May unlocked the best in that trio and helped those players become lottery picks. With Wolf and Goldin, Michigan went from the bottom of the Big Ten to the Sweet 16 in May's first season at the high-major level. In Dallas' final preseason game, May rolled out an even larger starting lineup of Kyrie Irving, Risacher, Flagg, PJ Washington and Daniel Gafford. While it's unclear if Risacher will be a long-term option at the 2 in that lineup, May's experience working with unorthodox lineups could bode well for the former No. 1 overall pick to establish a clear-cut role heading into his third NBA season.
A failed trade was the beginning of the end for Knecht in L.A.On Nov. 19, 2023, Knecht had a breakout performance against the Utah Jazz in the NBA Cup, knocking down nine 3-pointers and finishing with 37 points in 38 minutes during a dramatic 124-118 win. That moment should've been viewed as a coming-out party that established him as a key member of L.A.'s rotation for years to come.Instead, it was the beginning of the end. Less than three months later, Knecht was included in a trade package — alongside picks — to land Mark Williams from Charlotte. The trade came days after the Lakers stunned the NBA world by acquiring Luka Dončić in a deal that sent Anthony Davis back to Dallas. The trade for Williams — which cost the Lakers their promising rookie — was to give Dončić a long-term answer at the center position.But the trade was rescinded days later after Williams failed a physical exam with the Lakers. From that moment on, Knecht's career and outlook with the Lakers were murky at best. He has been a constant fixture in the trade rumor mill since almost being traded to Charlotte and has floated in and out of the Lakers' rotation.
On the days before the 2024 Draft, I thought Knecht being a top 10 pick was one of the lone guarantees from a class with plenty of unknowns. Knecht was the best transfer in college basketball during the 2023-24 season and established himself as one of the top shot creators and shooters in the class. On draft night, though, Knecht slid all the way to pick No. 17. At the time, he was considered one of the steals of the year. Knecht did struggle in summer league weeks later, but the signs from the start of his rookie year backed up the claim that he would outperform his draft slot.After appearing in just 54 games (and averaging just over 10 minutes per contest), that no longer appears to be the case. When asked about Knecht's future ahead of the Lakers' final preseason game, JJ Redick was blunt when asked what had changed since his rookie season."I think the biggest thing is the team changed," Redick said last week. "The team changed. Needs changed, the fit changed. I think he's gotten better as a player the last two years. I think, particularly last year, each guy got plenty of opportunities with the injuries we had. I just think coming into this year, we added a lot of wings and he's in a tough spot right now."
Why did teams move on from their rookies so quickly?From the first top 20 picks of the 2024 Draft, seven players have been traded or cut. However, there is no one-size-fits-all reason why a team decided to trade said player.Zaccharie Risacher (No. 1): He wasn't going to be part of the rotation going forward. The writing was on the wall after a shaky postseason.Rob Dillingham (No. 8): Dillingham has already been traded twice in 2026. The Timberwolves sent the one-time Kentucky star to the Bulls at the deadline. Then he was flipped again last month to the Hornets before being waived. It just hasn't worked out for Dillingham, an undersized guard who can't shoot. He remains a free agent heading into the season.Cody Williams (No. 10): Williams was a promising prospect coming out of Colorado. The younger brother of Thunder star Jalen Williams received some buzz as a potential No. 1 pick in a wide-open class due to his archetype. However, he was never able to find a consistent role with Utah and was traded to Minnesota earlier this offseason.Devin Carter (No. 13): Carter's rookie season got off to a rough start. After undergoing shoulder surgery right after the draft, Carter didn't play in the summer league or preseason and missed the start of the 2023-24 season. Carter was buried in Sacramento's guard rotation and never found consistent minutes. He was salary-dumped to the Hawks earlier this offseason before being waived. Carter is now on a two-way deal with the Celtics.Kel'el Ware (No. 15): Ware has shown flashes of being one of the best players from the class throughout his time with Miami. Now, he will look for a fresh start in Milwaukee after being part of the blockbuster trade that sent Antetokounmpo to the Heat.Jared McCain (No. 16): Former 76ers general manager Daryl Morey said they "sold high" on McCain when they traded him to Oklahoma City. McCain's rookie season with Philadelphia got off to a fantastic start before suffering a season-ending injury. McCain kept it up with the Thunder and is one of the best players from the class.Dalton Knecht (No. 17): Knecht was considered one of the most NBA-ready players in the class. He has lived up to that bill, at times, but inconsistent minutes with the Lakers — and the failed trade to Charlotte — were indicative of what was to come.One notable player who is set to be on his team's roster on Opening Night is former No. 6 pick Tidjane Salaün. The Hornets needed to cut one player to reach the 15-man roster limit and decided to waive veteran guard Pat Connaughton instead. Salaün was projected to go late-lottery on draft night. Instead, Charlotte selected him with the No. 6 pick. The phrase "two years away from being two years away" applies to Salaün, although he has shown signs of growth throughout his career. He is still just 21, but it's still a long shot that he plays meaningful minutes for the Hornets this season.Is there still hope for the 2024 class?Our CBS Sports Top 100 rankings tell the story about the stars of this class. Castle is part of a title contender with the Spurs and has the claim as the best — and most accomplished — player in the class so far. Mitchell, though, looks primed for a larger role with Oklahoma City this season and has legit breakout potential after a fantastic postseason.
Sarr looks like an ideal fit alongside Anthony Davis in Washington's frontcourt. His calling card in the pre-draft process was his defense, and he has certainly met expectations on that front: he averaged 2 blocks and 0.8 steals last season and could be in line to increase those numbers this season.Another player in this class who has flown under the radar is Jaylen Wells. The former second-round pick — who was selected right after Mitchell — started 69 games for Memphis last season and averaged 12.5 points, 3.2 assists, and 1.6 rebounds. Notably, Wells was the lone second-round pick to land on an All-Rookie team.The player to keep an eye on this season is Sheppard, who was thrown into a larger role last season after Fred VanVleet suffered a season-ending torn ACL weeks before the start of the 2025-26 campaign. Sheppard appeared in all 82 regular-season games and made 21 starts. He also started five of Houston's six playoff games, but averaged just under 30% from the 3-point line on 54 total attempts.
Sheppard's calling card coming out of Kentucky was his shooting. He was arguably the best 3-point shooter in college basketball during his lone college season. He did take strides from his rookie season (33.8%) to his sophomore year (39.4%) in the NBA from beyond the arc, but his first two seasons have been inconsistent for a former top-three pick.With Houston getting VanVleet back, it should take some of the pressure off Sheppard, but this will be an important year, as he is eligible for a rookie-scale extension next summer.Is the 2024 Draft a cautionary tale for next summer's draft?Major lottery reform is coming to the NBA this season. The new 3-2-1 format is designed to combat tanking and make the regular season more competitive after an epic tank race last season that saw the Wizards, Jazz, Grizzlies and Bulls jump into the top four.
There are plenty of unknowns about how the 2027 NBA Draft will ultimately stack up, but the early returns suggest NBA fans and teams should keep an eye on 2028 as the class that will be worth being "bad" for. Names to know for 2027 include Kansas' Tyran Stokes, Arkansas' Jordan Smith Jr. and Arizona's Caleb Holt. All great players, but it will be hard to rival what we witnessed last year —and even in 2025 — as far as draft classes go.Does that mean the 2027 Draft will have the same lack of consensus as 2024? Maybe. It's far too early to tell. Stokes is the consensus No. 1 prospect in the 2027 class heading into the season. However, if Duke big man Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje were eligible for the 2027 Draft — and he's not because he doesn't meet the draft's age requirement — the 7-foot-2 forward would be the consensus top-ranked prospect.

                    Adam Finkelstein                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
After back-to-back stacked draft classes, this upcoming draft could rival the 2024 class, but it's far too early to tell. The teams that got lottery luck in 2025 and 2026 should be thanking their lucky stars. The Hawks, unfortunately, won the lottery in a draft class that probably only stacks up to 2013.It's why Risacher is already on a new team and several others in the class have been traded. The 2024 class was set up to fail from the jump, and history suggests it might not get much better.

The Eagles quarterback is clinically stable and expected to make a full recovery, but he cannot participate in contact activities
